input:
You are a critic of research topics. Below are topic candidates for a study that an AI agent will carry out autonomously. Point out the weaknesses of each candidate.

The main readers of this study are researchers working on the social problem addressed and practitioners in government, business, communities and other settings (both humans and AIs). A good topic is one where readers' understanding or judgment changes between before and after reading the results. Each study takes 12 hours and is carried out within the range of local compute, public data and a small amount of AI API use.

For each candidate, look for weaknesses from the following points of view.
1. Effect on readers: Which understanding or judgment, concretely, would researchers and practitioners who read the results change? If they would not change any, say so.
2. Generality: Do the results hold beyond a particular tool, library version or dataset? Will they not become outdated in a few months?
3. Realism: Is there a risk that the effect appears only under artificial conditions or with inputs that are rare in reality? Are realistic inputs excluded from the targets?
4. Novelty: Is there close prior work or a known result (including what is already known from official statistics, reports or white papers)? Does it amount to no more than re-confirming a known concern with numbers?
5. Unpredictability: Could the result be largely predicted without experiments?
6. Size of the question: Has it become a solid but small question?

Before naming close prior work, confirm it by web search. Also look for literature and preprints from 2025 onward. Include the standard methods and classic studies of the field. Also check whether the same problem has been studied under a different name in other fields.

For each candidate, write in the following format.
- The most serious weakness (with the number of the point of view above)
- Prior work that seems close (authors, title, year, URL; write "unconfirmed" for any you could not confirm by web search)
- A scenario in which the value would be small even if it succeeds
- A direction that broadens the question or brings it closer to reality (at most one, within the scope of that candidate; do not propose new topics)

Do not rank the candidates. You have not been told which candidate is planned to be adopted.

Candidate list:
C01. Question: Do nearest neighbours in annual satellite embeddings preserve wetland water regimes when selecting geographically separate reference sites, and can explicit hydrological constraints prevent mismatches?
Method outline: Use public annual AlphaEarth embeddings and, if accessible, independently trained TESSERA embeddings, with US National Wetlands Inventory water-regime labels. Retrieve candidate reference sites within the same vegetation-structure class and with a geographic exclusion buffer; compare raw cosine retrieval, nearest geographic and random references, stronger hydrological-covariate matching, and supervised information/metric checks. Measure held-out water-regime agreement and selective retrieval across regions/years. Treat inventory agreement as a necessary screening condition, not restoration success or field-validated hydrology.
Closest prior work and difference: Brown et al. (2025), AlphaEarth Foundations, arXiv:2507.22291, evaluates scarce-label mapping and supervised decoders. Heiman (2026), Characterizing Brazilian Atlantic Forest Restoration Outcomes with Geospatial AlphaEarth Embeddings, arXiv:2605.05547, uses cosine similarity to reference forests as a restoration trajectory measure. Wen (2026), Streamlining Wetland Vegetation Mapping with AlphaEarth Embeddings, doi:10.3390/rs18020293, applies supervised vegetation classification; its full-text check is incomplete. Liu et al. (2026), Geospatial Foundation Embeddings as Transferable Catchment Descriptors, doi:10.1029/2026GL122814, and arXiv:2601.01558 address hydrological transfer between basins. The proposed narrow difference is testing external water-regime preservation of direct wetland reference retrieval conditional on vegetation, rather than supervised vegetation maps, runoff prediction, or prediction of embedding similarity itself. Existing ecological guidance already requires hydroperiod matching.

C02. Question: Can cross-year consistency constraints distinguish crop-rotation changes from changes in an annually updated satellite representation without fitting a new crop classifier each year?
Method outline: Compare transfer and consistency-constrained change alerts in annual published embeddings against repeated public crop labels with spatial and year holdouts.
Closest prior work and difference: Du et al. (2026), Utilising embeddings for maps of winter wheat and crop rotation in Henan China during 2018–2024, doi:10.5194/isprs-annals-XI-2-2026-865-2026, already evaluates limited-label temporal transfer and rotation mapping. Mandal et al. (2026), AG-STELLA: Spatio-Temporal Learning for Water-related Agricultural Land Use Activity Mapping with AlphaEarth, doi:10.24963/ijcai.2026/816, already uses temporal transition and hydroclimatic consistency. Brown et al. (2025), arXiv:2507.22291, includes change detection. The proposed difference is a lightweight diagnostic without retraining segmentation, but the substantive difference from those works remains uncertain.

C03. Question: Does improved marginal weather skill translate into useful estimates of simultaneous low-wind events across a regional backup portfolio?
Method outline: Compare coherent learned weather ensembles, marginally calibrated/reordered ensembles and climatological dependence baselines against reanalysis for joint low-wind events and fixed cost/loss backup decisions. The public catalogue currently requires an access application for saved research forecasts; no application or restricted-data access has been attempted.
Closest prior work and difference: Price et al. (online 2024 / Nature 2025), Probabilistic weather forecasting with machine learning, doi:10.1038/s41586-024-08252-9, already evaluates pooled forecasts and regional wind power. Schefzik, Thorarinsdottir and Gneiting (2013), Uncertainty Quantification in Complex Simulation Models Using Ensemble Copula Coupling, doi:10.1214/13-STS443, establishes dependence-preserving postprocessing. A spectral test of the butterfly effect and physical consistency in the diffusion-based GenCast’s ensembles (2026), doi:10.1038/s41612-026-01380-1, evaluates physical consistency. The proposed difference is specific joint-tail decision performance, not the known need for dependence, and data feasibility is unresolved.

C09. Question: Can short-record transferable probabilistic forecasts support municipal demand reserve decisions during unusual peaks, and does calibration with longer seasonal history change the decision?
Method outline: On the publicly licensed aggregate inflow series from the Battle of Water Demand Forecasting, compare small public pretrained forecasters against strong seasonal/local and quantile-regression methods. Hold out time periods; distinguish ordinary forecast accuracy, tail calibration and fixed reserve-loss criteria. No shortage consequence or human-user effect would be claimed.
Closest prior work and difference: Ansari et al. (2024), Chronos: Learning the Language of Time Series, arXiv:2403.07815, evaluates zero-shot probabilistic forecasting. Que, Gao and Qian (2024), Water demand forecasting in multiple district metered areas based on a multi-scale correction module neural network architecture, doi:10.1016/j.wroa.2024.100269, evaluates individual areas, totals and extreme conditions. Alvisi et al. (2025), Battle of Water Demand Forecasting, doi:10.1061/JWRMD5.WRENG-6887, already emphasizes multiple periods and metrics. Papacharalampous and Langousis (2022), Probabilistic Water Demand Forecasting Using Quantile Regression Algorithms, doi:10.1029/2021WR030216, supplies an established probabilistic approach. The proposed difference is the interaction between no-fitting short-record deployment and calibration using older seasonal history, rather than a generic forecast leaderboard.

C12. Question: How often do canopy-cover priorities for shade investment change after accounting for adjacent-tree geometry, and does global metre-scale height data reproduce those changes seen in lidar?
Method outline: Use public global canopy-height windows and public local lidar/land cover; compute fixed geometric shade screens and compare area priorities under global versus lidar heights. Include cover-only, geometry-aware and height-error sensitivity comparisons. Restrict claims to geometric screening; thermal comfort, health and user benefit would not be measured.
Closest prior work and difference: Tolan et al. (2024), Very high resolution canopy height maps from RGB imagery using self-supervised vision transformer and convolutional decoder trained on Aerial Lidar, arXiv:2304.07213, evaluates height and edges against lidar. Rahman et al. (2024), More than a canopy cover metric: Influence of canopy quality, water-use strategies and site climate on urban forest cooling potential, doi:10.1016/j.landurbplan.2024.105089, already establishes cover-only limitations. Meili et al. (2021), Vegetation cover and plant-trait effects on outdoor thermal comfort in a tropical city, doi:10.1016/j.buildenv.2021.107733, examines structural/trait effects. Wilkening et al. (2025), Canopy Temperature Reveals Disparities in Urban Tree Benefits, doi:10.1029/2024AV001438, combines cover and canopy condition. The proposed difference concerns whether global map errors change the geometry-based priorities that local lidar would give, rather than rediscovering the importance of shade or canopy quality.
